paragraphs.text: Chapter 1. Sleep

Sleep is the subject of the first chapter of this book because sleep profoundly impacts every aspect of our physiology and psychology. Put simply, sleep is the foundation of our mental health, our physical health, and our performance. We win by sleeping. I came to that realization pretty early but only because I struggled with sleep. As a kid I slept like a log—always a solid eight to nine hours, rarely waking up in the middle of the night even once. As a teen I would stay out late and sleep in on the weekends, as most of us did. I never thought about my sleep. When I reached my junior year in high school, however, everything changed. I would lie down, fall asleep right away, but then wake up three to four hours later, wide awake. Then I would toss and turn. Eventually I would fall back asleep but then needed to sleep really late into the morning to feel rested. School started at 8:00 a.m., so that wasn't an option most days. That had me falling asleep in class, feeling wide awake in the evening, and then the whole cycle would repeat.

Toward the end of high school when I started getting into fitness, I learned that we recover from exercise during sleep. That was the early 1990s and the public was not yet aware of the importance of sleep. There was some science on it—in fact some of the best work on the role of sleep for health and cognition was coming from the Stanford Sleep Lab just a few miles up the road from where I lived. But it was from a prominent trainer in the world of fitness that I first learned to take sleep seriously. He gave me one mostly good suggestion for sleep, and one terrible one. The mostly good suggestion was to read the work of Allan Hobson—a sleep researcher from Harvard—and I eventually did, although I discovered Allan's focus was mainly on the importance of dreams, which felt like a bit of a tease for someone with sleep issues. The terrible advice he gave me? He told me if I woke up in the middle of the night and couldn't fall back asleep that I should drink a half mug of white wine. I was seventeen! I tried it anyway, and it didn't work for me. Thankfully. We now know alcohol greatly reduces the quality and restorative properties of sleep, even if it does help some people fall asleep.

Eventually I figured out how to master the art of getting a great night's sleep, but it took time. Years, in fact. The science progressed too, of course, and we now know a lot about both the importance of sleep and ways to remedy pretty much any sleep issue. I wish I had the information you are about to read back in high school, and college, and graduate school, and my postdoc. The reality is, the busier we are, the more important sleep is to our health and performance. But no matter how busy or calm our life is, a great night's sleep is crucial to our mind and body. If you are like the majority of people, and you struggle to get a great night's sleep, you want to remedy that as soon as possible. But even if you are one of those rare individuals who sleeps deeply every night and wakes up feeling fully refreshed every day, there are still ways to improve your sleep and thus, your quality of life.

Perhaps you have heard some of this before. Most people know a bit about the benefits and importance of sleep. As I mentioned above, that is a fairly recent development. It was about a decade ago when Matthew Walker, who formerly directed the Center for Human Sleep Science at the University of California, Berkeley, and is currently at the University of Texas in Dallas, wrote the now famous book, Why We Sleep. At that time, the "I'll sleep when I'm dead" or the "I'll catch up on sleep this weekend" mentalities prevailed. Thanks in large part to Matt's book and other public education efforts, people now recognize they must sleep, yet the majority of people still don't sleep well and far too many people sleep poorly, with nearly half of adults reporting their sleep satisfaction as an "F"—meaning the lowest possible grade.

It is true that we all have slightly different sleep needs. Some of us consider ourselves morning larks. We prefer to rise early. Others are night owls who prefer to stay up late. These are what sleep researchers call chronotypes: genetically determined features of the chemicals, cells, and circuits that regulate when we prefer to go to sleep and wake up. You can blame your parents for your bedtime (and wake time) preference. Separate from your chronotype is the total amount of sleep you need. Some of us need six hours to feel fully rested, others need eight, and some people feel great with just five. I should point out, however, that the feel-great-on-five folks are exceedingly rare. Most people need seven to eight.

But as mentioned above, according to recent reports from the National Sleep Foundation and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), at least a third of Americans do not get nearly enough sleep—and that statistic is likely to be a vast underestimate given the enormous increase in time spent on social media and online nowadays. In fact, that figure skyrockets to more than 75 percent among high school students. That's right, approximately three-fourths of teens are not getting enough sleep, which is extremely concerning given that our adolescent and teen years are when much of our brain wiring related to mood and behavior regulation, as well as attention and learning, gets solidified. From birth until about age twenty-five is an especially sensitive and time-limited phase, or what is called a critical period. And the thing about critical periods is eventually they close: While our brains remain plastic our entire lives, the amount of neuroplasticity possible in those first twenty-five years far exceeds what is possible afterward, so teens can't simply make up for their lost brain wiring later on. We have no idea what the long-term consequences of this kind of chronic sleep deprivation are, but we do know that far too many young people are missing out on sleep at exactly the time when they need it most.

Compulsive overuse of phones and other screen-based technologies at night is a major factor for the poor sleep of adolescents and teens, but also for the poor sleep habits of adults. A central feature of life in the twenty-first century is to always be connected online and by text. So much so that by the classic definition of shift work, many—perhaps even most people—worldwide, now meet the definition of a shift worker, that is, awake for two to three hours between 10:00 p.m. and 5:00 a.m. Shift work is not just about staying up late but also involves reduced amounts of exposure to sunlight during the day, lack of sufficient darkness at night, and a nocturnally-shifted eating schedule. That has well-established negative health effects, including poor gut health, mental health deficits, and even decreased lifespan. So this is no trivial matter.

Smartphone technologies are not to blame per se, but when we use those technologies certainly is. We can scroll 24-7 and unless we resist, the light from our phone, tablet, or computer screen impairs our sleep. Not to mention that the content we absorb on those screens often affects our sleep, too, because of the elevated levels of arousal—aka stress—that content creates. Even if being on our phones or tablets in the hours before sleep doesn't stress us out, it can disrupt our sleep. We rarely hear how texting alters our sleep patterns but I would argue that for many people, it is at least as pernicious as social media in this regard. To be clear, texting is a wonderful tool for communication; it allows us to connect quickly. And social media can be a good source for learning, social connection, and entertainment. The downside, however, is that we can have conversations and observe events at any time of day or night. If we wake up in the middle of the night, we know we should roll over and go back to sleep, but many of us instead start reading and sending texts, or scrolling the internet or browsing social media.
SLEEP PROTOCOL View Sunlight as Soon as Possible After Waking
WHAT TO DO

• Get morning sunlight in your eyes as soon as possible after waking. Go outside and look in the direction of the sun for at least five to ten minutes each morning. Your goal should be to get sunlight in your eyes within the first thirty to sixty minutes of waking up.

• A few things to keep in mind. If you wake up before the sun rises, you'll obviously have to wait. If you can view the sun as it comes up across the horizon, great, but that's not vital for this protocol to work. Morning sunlight, as we will review, differs in quality from sunlight at other times of the day. It is best viewed by facing the sun without any physical barriers, like awnings or buildings, obscuring your view. Don't wear a brimmed hat, as it blocks some of the light that would otherwise reach your eyes from overhead. Wearing eyeglasses or contacts is fine but, alas, this protocol won't work nearly as well through a window or windshield, as that will filter out

I first learned about the importance of viewing morning sunlight from one of the world's preeminent sleep researchers, Seiji Nishino, MD, PhD. I was working in his lab at Stanford during a summer home from college, and I noticed he would always stop to face the sun for a few minutes before going into the lab for the day. Even if he arrived at the lab before sunrise (not uncommon for researchers in a sleep lab!), he would make sure to step outside shortly after sunrise and face the sun for a few minutes before returning to work. That was way back in 1996—when our understanding of the mechanisms of human circadian biology was rudimentary compared to now. Seiji explained that viewing morning sunlight felt good, that it gave him more energy for the day, and that it improved his sleep. I started joining him and joked that we resembled the many ground squirrels around us up on their haunches doing the very same thing. Little did I know that the exact same morning sunlight-sensing cells, circuits, and mechanisms were at play in us and those squirrels and, in fact, in every mammal where they have been examined. I quickly noticed that on days I viewed morning sunlight, I also felt good, had more energy for the day, and slept better at night, so I kept with it.

You should experience those benefits, too, because of the way morning sunlight—whether on a clear or cloudy day—kickstarts a powerful set of hormonal and neural mechanisms that positively shift the state of your entire brain and body for many hours afterward. It can work the first time and every time, and once you understand a bit about those mechanisms, it will allow you to easily adjust this protocol to your schedule and circumstances to derive the maximum benefits with minimal time investment.
Your Circadian Clock

Located a few centimeters above the roof of your mouth is a small cluster of neurons called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, or SCN. The SCN is your master circadian clock. Its job is to coordinate the activities of all the cells and organs in your body into a coherent twenty-four-hour rhythm so that certain cells and organs in your body are more active, and other cells and organs are less active, depending on the phase of that twenty-four-hour rhythm. The SCN keeps your body and brain on schedule.

The first documented discovery of a circadian clock came not from studies of humans or even of rodents, but of plants. In 1729, a French astronomer named Jean-Jacques d'Ortous de Mairan noticed that a mimosa plant kept in a totally dark room continued to rhythmically fold and unfold its leaves every twenty-four hours, just as if the sun was shining through the window. It was a mystery: If the plant was not unfurling to absorb sun or other light, then what was guiding its movements? About two hundred years later, German biologist Erwin Bünning tracked the movements of bean plant leaves and reported that they followed a cycle lasting 24.4 hours. Observations such as these confirmed that plants had internal, or what scientists call "endogenous," clocks that followed what later became known as... a circadian rhythm, named for the Latin circa diem, or "around a day."

And as decades of research would eventually confirm, the vast majority of organisms on Earth—not just plants but also insects, rodents, reptiles, and all mammals, including humans—have an endogenous timekeeper that keeps a twenty-four-hour circadian rhythm, even in the absence of any external cues about the status of the outside world. Our core body temperature, the release of certain hormones, and most notably our sleep-wake cycle, all follow a twenty-four-hour circadian rhythm. Even when scientists extracted individual cells from the body, the cells continued to follow this rhythm. And which genes they expressed and when, the proteins downstream of those genes, the cells' enzymatic activities—indeed not just some things but nearly everything about cellular function—appeared to vary, not randomly, but rather systematically every twenty-four hours. That was remarkable.

But what is equally remarkable is that all cells in our body can coordinate their individual rhythms in a manner that is timed perfectly with one another—like a well-practiced symphony, except this symphony involves not a few hundred or even a thousand participants, but trillions. And just like a symphony, it is not as if every cell simply needs to start and end its activity at the same time. Some cells need to be active at the same time, or in-phase with one another; some need to be active at opposite times, or in anti-phase, and still others repeat their cycles of activity faster, then slower, then faster, again with a unique signature and yet, still repeating once every twenty-four hours. They found that subjects generally spent about one-third of each twenty-four-hour period sleeping and two-thirds of it awake, just as most humans living aboveground do. However, the wake-up and to-sleep times of the people in the bunker drifted—they woke up slightly later and went to sleep slightly later each day. Thus, the bunker experiment confirmed the existence of a circadian rhythm, but one that requires some external cue to anchor it.

What remained mysterious was the biological basis of the circadian clock—was it a bloodborne factor? In the liver? In the brain? In the pineal gland? Theories abounded but none of them held up to experimentation. And another major question remained: In the environment outside the bunker, which external cues were responsible for setting that clock to a specific start and finish time each day?

Subsequent discoveries, first in rodents and later in humans, revealed the existence of a small cluster—or what is called a "nucleus"—of neurons located a few centimeters above our mouths that had a key part to play. It was later named the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) for "above the chiasm"—the chiasm being the location at the base of the brain where the nerve fibers from both eyes partially cross. As I mentioned earlier, the SCN is the master circadian clock: the structure that coordinates the activities of all our cells and organs. In other words, the SCN is the orchestra conductor that makes sure each cell's twenty-four-hour rhythm starts on time. In 1972, Irving Zucker's lab at UC Berkeley and Robert Moore's lab at the University of Chicago independently discovered that lesions to the SCN render organisms' circadian pattern arrhythmic and disorganized. Naturally occurring SCN lesions caused by tumors eventually showed the SCN is necessary for sleep-wake, hunger, and other bodily rhythms to obey circadian cycles in humans as well. Moreover, animal studies showed that transplanting even just a small number of healthy SCN neurons into an arrhythmic brain restored a coherent twenty-four-hour rhythm, proving the SCN is both necessary and sufficient for endogenous circadian rhythms.

If ever there was a brain structure whose function is beautifully organized to help ensure our survival as a species, it is the SCN. Even the SCN's seeming imperfection turns out to be perfect after all. Stay with me here. For example, the SCN generates a period—meaning a cycle length—that is close to but not quite twenty-four hours. The SCN's period tends to be a bit longer than that, up to 24.5 hours. By virtue of this, it can shift the start of the circadian rhythm forward or backward according to seasonal changes in day length or other survival-based needs, without making a mess and setting our cells on different schedules. In other words, allowing a little room in its period duration affords us more flexibility and overall precision, not less, which is great because as we all know life is rarely the same from one day to the next. What's more, it is also what allows for phase shifting, or the ability to change the start time of the daily cycle. If you're wondering why this doesn't have us waking up later and going to sleep later each day, it's because viewing morning light and evening light nudges your clock back and forth perfectly, to keep it regular. Later I'll explain how you can leverage that to overcome jet lag or any new schedule fast, but for now, all you need to know is that the not-exactly-twenty-four-hour rhythm is a feature, not a flaw.

As you probably already realize from the call to action that is Sleep Protocol 1, our SCN cares about whether it is light or dark out. And of course light-dark cycles are set by the spin of the earth. But how is it that our SCN—a tiny cluster of neurons embedded deep in the darkness of our brains—"knows" about the spin of the earth? Let's consider how to answer that question with insights from planetary science and cosmology. We're all on this big sphere in space, spinning around at about one thousand miles per hour, causing us to face the sun, then away from the sun, then back toward the sun every twenty-four hours. Because the earth is round, the exact duration of sunlight we can experience each day depends, of course, on where we happen to be on earth. The variability is large, ranging from rather equal light-dark splits at the equator to nearly full days and/or nights of darkness or sunlight exposure at the poles. But no matter where we are on earth, inside each of our brains, our SCN steadily churns out that slightly longer than twenty-four-hour rhythm of coordinated cellular activity across our whole body. Ultimately it is our SCN that tells us when to sleep and when to wake. We are a diurnal, not a nocturnal, species. We can stay up late and sleep all day if we choose, but even for

optic nerves convey electrical signals about the presence or absence of sunlight, objects, faces, moving vehicles, and on and on to different brain areas, including—you guessed it—the SCN. The connections between your eyes and your brain are truly a spectacular product of biological engineering. First, they solve the problem of how to inform image-forming regions of your brain about "what is out there" in the world, so you can see faces, moving objects, and colors. They also solve the problem of letting your SCN know "when it is out there" in the world, by the presence of sunlight.

The neurons that convey the presence of sunlight to the SCN are not of the image-forming kind; they don't respond to the shape of the sun, but instead to its brightness and to the specific wavelengths of sunlight that reach your eyes when the sun is low in the sky. We refer to these specific wavelengths as low solar angle sunlight. Have you ever noticed that low solar angle sunlight appears more yellow than midday sun? Or even orange? Check out a sunrise or sunset and compare the color of sunlight to the color of sunlight at noon. Of course, sunlight doesn't change according to where it is in the sky, but what portions of sunlight are visible to us does. Sunlight is always full spectrum: It contains all wavelengths of light, red-orange-yellow-green-blue-indigo-violet, or ROYGBIV, just as they taught us in elementary school. The R(ed), O(range), and Y(ellow) are longer wavelengths of light, the G(reen) is medium wavelength, and the B(lue), I(ndigo), and V(iolet) are shorter wavelengths. And of course, the sun emits UV and far-red, or infrared wavelengths, too, but we can't see those (although many other animals and insects can). When the sun is high in the sky, it appears white, because all the wavelengths of light arrive at our eyes at roughly the same intensities. When the sun is low in the sky, we see the sun as more yellow, orange, or red, because molecules in the atmosphere preferentially redirect the shorter blue, indigo, and violet wavelengths of light—a process called Rayleigh scattering. (We'll discuss the properties of light in depth in chapter 5.)

All mammals, us humans included, have evolved a special system of light detection that responds specifically to the presence and contrast of short and long wavelengths of bright light, which is exactly what reaches your eyes if you view sunlight early or late in the day, while the sun is fairly low in the sky. In other words, we all have a sunrise and sunset detecting system in our eyes that communicates the time of day to our SCN.

As I mentioned earlier, this timekeeping eye-to-brain circuit is also a fairly recent discovery. And by recent, I mean recent: In the late 1990s, there still wasn't general agreement among circadian biologists whether light—and not some other cue like social interactions—was the dominant force entraining our SCN. Then, in 1998, neuroscientist Ignacio "Iggy" Provencio made a key discovery. Iggy found a molecule in the skin of an African frog species that caused its skin to darken when exposed to sunlight was also present in the eyes of mice. The molecule was an opsin, which is a kind of protein that absorbs light, and when it does, it changes its conformation to set off a signaling cascade. Since the same opsin was known to cause darkening of dermal melanophores in frog skin, Provencio called the mouse retinal opsin melanopsin. Other labs confirmed melanopsin-containing cells are abundant in the human retina, too, mostly in the lower portion that views the upper visual field, which, you might have guessed, corresponds to the sky.

So we have a frog-skin-like set of cells in our eyes? Not quite. To explain what makes melanopsin-containing retinal cells so special, first a bit about photoreceptors. Photoreceptors are neurons that convert light into electrical signals the rest of the retina and brain can interpret. But the retinal cells that contain melanopsin are not like other photoreceptors. The melanopsin-containing retinal neurons Iggy discovered turned out to be both photoreceptive and retinal ganglion cells—the neurons that connect the eyes to the brain and the very cells whose wirelike extensions, or axons, make up the optic nerves. Soon after, a group of neuroscientists, David Berson and Felice Dunn at Brown University and Samer Hattar and King-Wai Yau at Johns Hopkins University, along with several of their students and postdocs, confirmed that melanopsin RGCs send their axons to the SCN and that they fire electric signals, thereby releasing neurotransmitters, when light is shone on them. Remarkably, they did this when they were isolated from all other retinal cells. As long as the light shone was very bright and long lasting, they fired electrical signals. Doing so activates the ipRGC-to-SCN circadian entrainment circuit and initiates dozens of beneficial processes that get and keep your brain and body going throughout the day. And toward the evening, it puts you in the best possible position to get a great night's sleep.

In fact, we have copious evidence that this is foundational to both our daytime well-being and nighttime sleep. As one small example, a group of architects and neurologists came together in 2014 to investigate how windowless offices affected the people who worked in them. They asked twenty-seven office workers who had either no windows, or work areas situated far from windows, and twenty-two people working in offices with windows, about their well-being and sleep quality. The questionnaire scores were decidedly poorer among the windowless workers. They reported more sleep disturbances and an overall unsatisfactory quality of sleep.

In the early 2000s, a group of chronobiologists (scientists who study biological timing) at the Institute for Medical Psychology, in Munich, Germany, surveyed five hundred people about their sleep times, light exposure, and chronotype—as in, morning person, night owl, et cetera (you'll find out how to determine yours in Sleep Protocol 4). They found that the amount of light exposure during the day correlated with what time people went to bed: More exposure during the day meant earlier bedtimes. This link can be partly explained by external factors, like employment: People whose livelihoods depend on being outdoors are more likely to be early-to-bed types, especially if their work requires them to rise early or is physically demanding. But that doesn't explain the connection entirely. It turns out that it's also due, in part, to the fact that exposure to daylight has a regulating effect on our physiology—causing elevated levels of alertness by a host of different pathways, including hormonal and neural pathways. As one review put it, "In sum, research seems to agree that daylight (at high intensities) is beneficial for sleep." There are also numerous studies showing that bright-light exposure early in the day—at the intensities that one would get from being outdoors in the morning—is beneficial for everything from mood to hormone health, daytime energy levels, and on and on.

But before you say, "Okay, got it!," there's just a bit more to understand about the underlying mechanisms in this protocol, and that's the relationship between sleep and wakefulness. And it will help you get the most out of this protocol, regardless of where you live and the time of year.

Our daytime levels of alertness reflect the quality and duration of our nighttime sleep. That's a giant "duh." We all know that if we sleep poorly, we drag both mentally and physically the next day. We also all know that if we sleep great, we're focused and motivated to do all kinds of things that require energy... and that we have the energy to do them. But what most people do not know is that the relationship between sleep and wakefulness works in the other direction too. When we are alert during the morning and daytime, we are more likely to expend mental and physical energy that in turn helps us sleep at night. Even those of us who sleep well typically find that increasing our daytime physical activity—especially in the hours between sunrise and 2:00 p.m.—leads to significantly better sleep, which in turn leads to more energy the next day, which improves sleep, and so on. Again, you're probably thinking, "This is common knowledge. Do we really need science to explain this?" Here is the lesser-known fact: Morning sunlight viewing is the best way to increase our morning and daytime energy levels. Not food (although fine to eat early in the day), not caffeine (also fine). It's morning sunlight.

Morning sunlight increases your energy levels through at least three different mechanisms. First, it suppresses any residual melatonin you may have circulating in your brain (Sleep Protocol 3 includes an extensive look at melatonin, a hormone that helps promote sleepiness). As discussed above, when the ipRGCs are activated by sunlight viewing, they send electrical signals to the SCN. The SCN, in turn, stimulates a collection of neurons in the nearby paraventricular nucleus, or PVN. The PVN then sets off a cascade of signals that go through the spinal cord and back up to the pineal gland in the brain, shutting off melatonin production. Voila! You've suppressed the primary hormone that promotes sleepiness by viewing morning sunlight.

Second, bright light reaching your eyes helps suppress the action of adenosine, a chemical that also leads to feelings of sleepiness. Sunlight does this indirectly via its effects on other systems in the brain and body, but nonetheless, it has a potent adenosine-reducing effect. (We'll take a deep dive into adenosine in Sleep Protocol 7). After a full night's sleep, adenosine levels tend to be low, but if you happen to not get enough sleep (as so many of us do), morning light helps reduce any residual adenosine. That both increases your alertness and prevents the residual adenosine from delaying your circadian clock, which would otherwise bias you toward waking up later the next day, then going to sleep later, then waking up even later the following day, and so on (what chronobiologists call a phase delay). Such circadian "drift" brought on by mild sleep deprivation is very common. It is best remedied by viewing morning sunlight to reset your circadian rhythm.

Third, we need to talk about cortisol. Because it's often discussed in the context of chronic stress, which is bad, most people think cortisol is "bad" too. But it's not bad. Cortisol is essential to health and your levels of energy—you just don't want your cortisol levels to be elevated at the wrong times. Your SCN is located in your hypothalamus (H), which is part of a biological circuit that also includes your pituitary gland (P), a small, stalklike protrusion at the base of your brain that releases hormones into your bloodstream. The circuit also includes your adrenal glands (A), which reside atop your kidneys. This circuit is known as the HPA axis. The HPA axis is one of the main systems that responds to stress (which is why you'll hear more about it in chapter 3). Here's how it works: It starts with signals from the hypothalamus, which then stimulate the release of specific hormones from the pituitary, which in turn stimulate adrenaline and cortisol release from your adrenals.

Cortisol levels generally stay low and continue to drop in the evening and at nighttime (assuming it doesn't spike from stress or intense exercise—more on that below), and then it falls to its nadir in those first four to five hours of sleep before starting to rise again toward morning. We return to this circadian cortisol curve in chapter 3, and the role it plays in promoting health in women and men of all ages. For now, the key thing to know is that for cortisol to support our health, it needs to peak in the first hour or so after waking; it then needs to drop precipitously in the evening and night and continue falling to reach its nadir in those initial four to five hours of sleep. Viewing morning sunlight doesn't directly cause the morning peak in cortisol, but it can dramatically amplify its rise by as much as 50 percent. This also helps ensure that this peak comes early in the day and isn't shifted to the afternoon. Late-day elevations in cortisol have negative consequences over time such as sleeplessness, anxiety, and metabolic disease.

A quick note: A morning workout, morning caffeine, and breakfast (provided it isn't a huge and/or carbohydrate-laden one) will all promote wakefulness, too, and thereby contribute to a well-aligned circadian rhythm. But morning sunlight is the most potent lever for increasing morning cortisol and thus energy during your day, and for improving your sleep at night. Don't underestimate its power. Keep your circadian rhythm attuned to the sun, and all of these mechanisms will work as they should.
FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS
It's often dark when I wake up. What do I do if I have no access to morning sunlight but I want to start my day?

If you wake up before sunrise, and you want to start your day, I suggest turning on as many bright indoor lights in your home—or hotel room, or wherever you may be—as possible. Sunlight cannot be replaced by standard indoor lighting, but turning on indoor lighting first thing won't hurt. Then get outside to view morning sunlight once the sun is up.

If you wake before sunrise every day, or if you live in a part of the world where it is very dark in winter, you may want to invest in a 10,000 lux light to help ensure you get enough light in the morning (lux is a measure of brightness). Most cost about $100, and some are portable for travel. I often wake up before sunrise, and because the ipRGCs can be activated by very bright artificial lights if those bright lights include sufficient short wavelengths, I keep a 10,000 lux lamp in my kitchen and bathroom. It lacks long wavelength light, so I also have a red incandescent light next to it and I turn that on too. I use the red incandescent light from SaunaSpace (no affiliation). I turn them both on first thing in the morning and then I get outside to view morning sunlight once the sun is up. I am well aware these lights are not a replacement for sunlight, but they help bridge the gap until the sun is up. Once the sun is up, you can be sure I go outside to view it! And I will sometimes keep the 10,000 lux lamp and a red incandescent light on and facing me for an hour or so once I'm back working at my desk or getting ready for the day. Chapter 5 further explains the logic and benefits of this extended morning light exposure. There I also mention options that can be of real help for sleep as well as other aspects of health too, such as metabolic health.

But remember, morning sunlight is the best stimulus for your ipRGCs, SCN, and circadian rhythm, and it costs nothing! Figure out how to view it each morning. Again, you don't need to see it cross the horizon as it rises. If you do, great, but if you wake up after sunrise, that's fine. Do your best to view sunlight within the first thirty to sixty minutes after waking up. Bring your coffee or tea outside with you. Bring your spouse or kids if they're awake. Bring your dog if you have one. Remember, dogs, cats, cows, and other animals have ipRGCs and an SCN, too, and they benefit from morning sunlight in many of the same ways and via the same mechanisms as we do.
What if it's cloudy outside?

To activate your ipRGCs fastest, go outside and face east toward the sun on a nice, clear morning with no clouds in the sky. Obviously, this isn't possible for everyone every day. Again, fortunately, sparse clouds do not interfere with the interaction between sunlight and our circadian clock. However, if the sky is densely overcast and gray, a 10,000 lux light can be a real help, but still aim for getting more sunlight in your eyes to compensate for the lower intensity of sunlight and reduced yellow-blue contrast exposure you're likely to get on very overcast days. In fact, it's especially important that you get sunlight in your eyes on overcast days. This is for three reasons: (1) dense clouds reduce the number of photons reaching your eyes in a given amount of time; (2) they filter out much of the longer (yellow, orange, and red) wavelengths of light, and (3) you are likely to be indoors more on cloudy days, which can cause the SCN to fall out of sync with the solar cycle, which leads to later nights, more artificial light exposure at night, more circadian disruption, and so on.

Aim to extend the sunny, clear day recommendation of a minimum of five to ten minutes, to at least fifteen minutes on cloudy days, and thirty minutes (minimum) on densely overcast days. That may seem like a long time, but remember, you don't need to stand in one place gazing at the sky. Take a walk. Make a call. Listen to a book or podcast or talk to a friend, partner, or other family member. The intricacies of what happens when we sleep—the so-called architecture of sleep—deserves a book of its own, and indeed many have been written about it. Rarely discussed, however, is how the architecture of each sleep-wake cycle influences our sleeping and our waking states. We touched on this topic a bit earlier in this chapter. The Stages of Sleep

Many people are familiar with the two major types of sleep: rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, and non-REM sleep. Non-REM sleep is often referred to as deep or slow-wave sleep, but that's oversimplified. Non-REM sleep consists of three distinct phases that we enter, one after the other. These are referred to as N1, N2, and N3 sleep, and only in the N3 stage does actual deep or slow-wave sleep occur. Cycling through N1, to N2, to N3, to REM sleep takes, on average, about ninety minutes. So a person who sleeps for three hours might make it through two cycles, a person who sleeps for six hours experiences four cycles, and a person who sleeps 7.5 hours gets five cycles, and so on.

We enter N1, or light sleep, first and it typically lasts five to ten minutes. It is easy to rouse us from N1 sleep. But N1 is not merely a transition stage; during N1, our body starts to generate additional adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, the chemical that fuels all our biological processes. What's more, proteins that have become misshapen or broken during our waking hours get repaired during N1, and proteins that help build memories by reconfiguring our neural circuits are created.

Next we enter N2 sleep, which lasts about twenty minutes. During N2 our body temperature drops, our heart rate slows down, and our brain produces sleep spindles—surges of transient brain activity that help consolidate information we have learned in the days prior. Sleep spindles are vital for learning new cognitive information and motor skills, which both represent types of neuroplasticity. We explore this in greater detail in chapter 6. N2 has another intriguing feature: PGO waves, which are surges of large-scale brain activity that travel from the pons (P) of the brainstem, to the geniculate (G), a structure in our thalamus (the sensory waystation we discussed earlier), and then to our occipital (O) cortex, which resides in the back of our brain and is involved in, among other things, visual processing. PGO waves trigger the release of massive amounts of glutamate, an excitatory neurotransmitter that is a requisite component of the multistage process of learning, such as in the formation and elimination of synapses.

After N1 and N2 we enter deep sleep, what sleep researchers call slow-wave sleep, or N3. This is an extremely restorative stage of sleep. During N3, our brain waves shift to very high amplitude and low frequency, aka slow; our heart rate slows way down, and growth hormone is released from our pituitary gland into our bloodstream. What's more, the active repair of our muscle, brain, and other bodily tissues occurs—including our tendons, skin, heart, et cetera. That process involves a lot of protein synthesis, or the repair and regeneration of cells and tissues by use of specific amino acids. Some of that repair and regeneration occurs in response to tissue damage from exercise, but most of it is simple "housekeeping"-based cellular turnover and repair, which is also vital to our health and longevity. N3 is also when glymphatic washout of our brain occurs. This process was discovered just in the past fifteen years or so and involves the pulsing of lymph-like fluid through our brain, thereby removing the waste products caused by normal brain metabolism and any cellular debris that accumulated the previous day. This glymphatic clearance is actively governed by multiple brain regions—including the locus coeruleus—that we will talk about more below and in later chapters.

REM sleep, or rapid eye movement sleep, follows N3, but often we cycle from N3 back to N2 for a few minutes or more before advancing into REM sleep. REM sleep is crucial for sorting through all that waking life brings our way by eliminating or strengthening specific neural connections in accordance with what information we need to keep and what we should discard. Thus, think of REM sleep as an experience audit, with only the meaningful experiences surviving the cut.

One more interesting thing about REM: Our body becomes mostly paralyzed during this stage, a phenomenon known as sleep atonia. The most prevalent hypothesis to explain sleep atonia is that it keeps us from acting out our dreams during REM sleep. Our brains are extremely active during REM and the dreams we experience during this stage tend to be vivid and emotionally laden—often marked by flying, swimming, being filled with anxiety or awe, and highly dynamic in how we move through time and space (in the dream of course). The idea is that REM-associated atonia prevents us from acting in accordance with what are essentially in-sleep hallucinations, which would put us in danger.

The relative amount of time we spend in REM sleep increases, and the amount spent in deep N3 sleep decreases, as we complete more sleep cycles across a night of sleep. This means our most vivid dreams tend to occur as we approach morning. A baby's sleep is largely REM sleep, and the amount of REM we experience decreases with age starting in adolescence. If we are sleep-deprived, or we do something that reduces the amount of REM sleep we get on a given night—using cannabis, for instance—the next night we experience REM rebound by entering REM sleep sooner in the sleep cycle, and experiencing more REM overall. Health risks of sleep deprivation

Given all this, it becomes clearer and clearer how lack of sleep, but also altered sleep architecture, affects our mind and body in a variety of ways. Sleep deprivation is associated with diminished response time, alertness, attention, memory, and executive functioning. Additionally, as described at the chapter outset, lack of sleep can bring about longer-term problems as well. Insufficient REM sleep may increase the risk of dementia. In 2017, a group of researchers published their investigation of links between dementia and sleep architecture. They looked at three years of data on thirty-two adults over age sixty with dementia and found that the likelihood of cognitive decline fell in line with a reduction in REM sleep. In fact, with every 1 percent reduction in REM sleep, the risk of dementia rose by about 9 percent. (Non-REM sleep deprivation did not share this connection.) The role of REM in building and consolidating neural connections, thereby protecting against cognitive decline, may also explain why truncating this stage would raise the risk of dementia, but direct evidence for this mechanism in humans is still lacking.

Getting sufficient REM sleep is also connected to overall longevity. In 2020, a group of researchers from multiple institutions reported that less REM sleep is associated with an increased mortality risk. Using data from 4,050 people, they found that for every 5 percent decrease in REM sleep, the mortality rate increased by 13 percent. That held true for most causes of death, including cardiovascular disease. Ask any sleep researcher "How can I get more REM sleep?" and they will tell you "Sleep in an extra hour or two." But most people can't afford to sleep in an extra hour or two past their usual wake-up time.

The good news is that when we sleep is almost as important as getting enough of it. If we get to bed and wake up at a time that is in sync with our chronotype, we end up getting more growth hormone release, and we spend less time in light sleep and more time in deep sleep and REM sleep. As a consequence, we tend to need less sleep overall. Our sleep can become more efficient and restorative.

Working at nighttime and sleeping in the daytime is associated with greatly elevated risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression, and suicide. Shift workers are also susceptible to neurocognitive impairment and at greater risk for substance abuse. One large survey from Canada found that executive function is significantly worse among people whose jobs take place outside normal work hours. One study found the level of performance impairment to be equal to a blood alcohol concentration of 0.10, which exceeds the legal limit for driving in many places. To be clear: Being a night owl is not the same thing as forcing yourself to be nocturnal, so if that's your chronotype, don't worry. The health detriments of shift work are likely to be multifactorial—the lack of sunlight, the altered social interactions associated with an inverted schedule, and more. We know that one of the worst types of shift work for one's health is the swing shift, where people switch back and forth from daytime to nighttime work each week or even within the same week.

How long we sleep, when we sleep, and how consistent we are with our sleep-wake schedule affect our physical and mental health. That's why I hope you try the approach outlined here. Figure out what is best for you and then stick with it.

Many people wonder whether wake times should be later after that occasional late night. If you usually go to sleep somewhere between 8:30 and 11:00 p.m. and have a night where you're up until 1:00 or 2:00 a.m., should you sleep late or wake up at your usual time? What about children and teenagers?

The advice is a little different for young children and teenagers. Babies need to sleep A LOT and enter REM far more frequently and for longer than any other age group. Toddlers and young children should also sleep as much or as often as necessary, or desired, to support their extraordinarily fast brain and bodily growth rates. The amount of neuroplasticity in infants and children, all the way up to adolescence and beyond, is incredible—and sleep is a key part of that process. Limiting their sleep is never recommended but of course once kids are in school, setting a regular schedule (and keeping devices out of their rooms near bedtime and throughout the night) becomes important.

Sleep needs are somewhat different for teenagers. Bedtimes shift during puberty for at least two known reasons. First is what researchers call the homeostatic sleep drive. This term refers to a brain and bodily pressure to sleep that builds up gradually throughout the day, mainly due to adenosine accumulation. The longer we are awake, the more adenosine in our bodies, and the greater the pressure to sleep. Adenosine levels drop while we sleep and begin to mount again when we wake up for the new day. This pressure to sleep is separate from the circadian clock mechanisms we have discussed a lot thus far. Teenagers (good rebels that they are) resist this pressure and force themselves to stay up late, building up more adenosine and, therefore, the desire to sleep in the next morning. And they often don't need to force themselves to stay up late; it just happens naturally, as the hormonal testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone surges of puberty shift their circadian clock to a later phase. Melatonin production begins later in the teenage brain than in the brains of either adults or younger children. All of these changes leave the typical sixteen-year-old awake until about 11:00 p.m. And this age group should be sleeping about nine hours per night, making 8:00 a.m. the preferred wake-up time.

Studies have found that moving school start times to 8:30 a.m. or later leads to better grades and other measures of academic performance. There is even evidence suggesting that this shift also reduces car crashes among teen drivers. It's beneficial for teenagers to have days when they can sleep as long as they want, even if that means staying in bed until noon. That doesn't mean they should never be woken up earlier on a Saturday or Sunday, but parents and caregivers do not need to worry about prolonged sleeping on the weekends. Teenagers, yes, reference this book if you need leverage to sleep in and parents, yes, you still want to encourage them to get sunlight in their eyes once they get up, even though it is midday, and not low-solar-angle sun.

Current data indicate that teenagers in the US are in the midst of an epidemic of sleep deprivation that is likely having serious consequences for their health. Ideally, young people between the ages of six and twelve years should sleep at least nine hours per night, and thirteen-to-eighteen-year-olds should sleep at least eight hours per night. More than 70 percent of young people do not sleep enough, according to one large survey from the CDC. Anxiety, mood disorders, obesity, high-risk behavior, poor academic performance, and substance use have all been tied to sleep deprivation among adolescents. Good practices for teenagers include shutting off screens at least an hour before bedtime, keeping the phone (and the laptop, the tablet, etc.) out of the bedroom at night and the room cool and dark, having a consistent bedtime, and, ideally, sleeping for those eight to nine hours per night.

Research has found that the ideal ambient temperature while we sleep is between approximately 66 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit, which typically brings the microclimate immediately around our skin down to somewhere between 88 and 95 degrees Fahrenheit. To fall asleep our core body temperature needs to decrease by about 1 to 2 degrees.

A lower core body temperature facilitates various sleep-related biological processes you are now familiar with. First, research indicates that this reduction may help initiate non-REM sleep, and our lowest body temperature is associated with deep sleep. Melatonin, a hormone that facilitates falling asleep, is released in sync with the nightly drop in body temperature. In one small study of twelve women who were entrained to the solar cycle, the secretion of natural melatonin at night occurred with a simultaneous decline in core body temperature. Other studies have observed a similar coupling.

The stillness of our body during early sleep also plays a role in further dropping our core body temperature. In sleep, our autonomic nervous system shifts from more sympathetic activity (or tone, as it's often referred to), which is related to being alert and able to generate movement, to a far more parasympathetic tone, which is associated with calmness, lower heart rate, and less or no bodily movement. All that combined causes our blood to flow more to our periphery, to our hands and feet, where it "dumps heat," which in turn leads to a lower core body temperature.

This means that warming up our hands and feet a bit before getting into bed could facilitate falling asleep. That may seem paradoxical: Why would warming up your periphery help at a time when cooling down your core body temperature is the goal? Because heating your periphery acts as a trigger. A hot shower or bath, or a sauna, warms the surface of your body. That causes the preoptic area of your hypothalamus—a brain area that works sort of like a thermostat—to trigger a compensatory response, lowering the core temperature in your body. This process makes it easier to fall asleep, a phenomenon known colloquially as the warm bath effect.

Once you get in bed, having your sleeping environment cool is also helpful. Many people sleep best in a cool room but with their whole body under loads of warm blankets. Other people run hot and like to sleep under just a sheet or a light blanket. Try out a few of these recommendations and pick what suits you best.

We know that napping can increase our ability to focus and learn. Matthew Walker, a professor of neuroscience and biomedical engineering at the University of Texas in Dallas, conducted a study in which a group of participants learned a new set of facts at midday. The finding goes back to the role of sleep spindles, which we covered in Sleep Protocol 4. These are the types of brain waves present during N2 sleep, which happens early in the sleep cycle. Even a brief snooze of twenty minutes takes us into N2. Sleep spindles help us process new learning, but also prepare our brain for more learning after we wake up.

Napping also influences our mood. In another study, Walker and his group asked participants to rate the level of emotion they observed in a photograph. How angry were the angry faces? Toward the end of the day, the non-nappers were rating the emotions as more extreme; angry people were angrier, and so on. Idling is clearly not neuroscientific language. Napping, on the other hand, lets our brain enter N1 and N2 sleep, allowing even lower frequency theta waves (4–8 Hz) to emerge. Experienced meditators can get themselves into a state where theta waves emerge quickly, although that takes practice. Self-directed relaxation protocols like NSDR are different. NSDR involves shifting our autonomic nervous system into a more parasympathetic, or relaxed, state by breathing in a manner in which the duration of our exhales is deliberately emphasized. NSDR also involves deliberately and systematically moving our focus of attention from one part of our body to another, then to locations far from our body, then closer to us, then away again. The focusing, then defocusing, and moving and resetting of attention over and over keeps the mind active. And because it is done while the body is deeply relaxed, it brings about a somewhat dreamlike state, and yet you are completely aware and alert.

NSDR is a modification of an ancient practice known as yoga nidra, which roughly translates to "yoga sleep." Yoga nidra has been described as creating the experience of moving our mind away "from thinking and doing toward a state of being and feeling"—which is an admittedly vague statement. There is a small but growing body of modern science on the brain and bodily states that yoga nidra and NSDR bring about and their ability to restore mental and physical vigor, improve consolidation of newly learned information, offset sleep loss, and more.

When I first tried yoga nidra in 2017, I found it to be incredibly restorative. Doing this technique for twenty to thirty minutes first thing in the morning after a restless or less-than-full night's sleep left me feeling fully rested, like I'd had the best sleep of my life. I also noticed that incorporating this practice in the morning improved my ability to fall back asleep quickly if I happened to wake up in the middle of the night. That's right—even though NSDR stands for non-sleep deep rest, and even though it is typically done in the morning or afternoon, something about doing it at that time significantly improved my ability to self-direct my brain and body into a relaxed state and drift back to sleep at night if ever I needed to. What's more, if I ever woke up in the middle of the night, listening to a guided NSDR recording beat tossing and turning, and often sent me back to sleep.

Challenges with falling asleep and staying asleep are very common, so I was intrigued. I also noticed that replacing an afternoon nap with an NSDR session left me feeling especially reinvigorated and did not alter my nighttime sleep in any negative way. I wondered how this simple practice really worked. So I dove into the literature and found there wasn't much known. But the few studies I did find were interesting. A 2002 study from Denmark found that doing yoga nidra dramatically increases levels of dopamine in a brain region called the basal ganglia, which are involved in taking, and withholding, action. Yoga nidra also reduced people's blood pressure and heart rate. Although this and other studies of yoga nidra were small in terms of the number of subjects studied, other investigations indicated that this practice could improve various measures of mental health and help consolidate certain forms of learning.

At one point, I decided to devote a portion of my lab to studying yoga nidra as a tool for stress reduction. To do so we needed to keep its core elements—breathing that emphasizes long exhales to slow the heart rate and place us into a more parasympathetic state, the deliberate and systematic movement of one's perceptual attention to the surface and then the interior of the body, then away from the body, and so on—but we opted to remove the "intentions" and any language pertaining to more spiritual aspects of yoga nidra. This parsing was not an attempt at cultural appropriation of an ancient tradition. Rather, it was a way to examine this powerful tool within the context of Western science, where we seek to understand what works and why, and to then use this knowledge to build more efficient and effective tools. Any aspect of the practice that couldn't be reliably measured was discarded.

Later, as I moved into public education and spoke about stress mitigation tools, I coined the term non-sleep deep rest, which keeps the key elements related to the physiology of yoga nidra, but removes the subjective aspects that are hard to keep constant from one person to the next. And eventually, given the wide interest in stress mitigation tools, my podcast team produced various NSDR scripts of short (ten minute), medium (twenty minute), and long (thirty minute) durations and made them freely available online. According to Hollingworth's report, published in the American Journal of Psychology in 1912, a few grains of caffeine taken on successive days were enough to impair sleep. The connection relied on self-reporting and each individual recording their impression about the quality of their sleep following each study day. But the findings were consistent. Decades later we know how that happens: Caffeine leads to longer sleep latency (that is, the time it takes to fall asleep) and more nighttime waking, thus leading to reduced wakefulness the next day. We also now know that caffeine can alter sleep architecture, including less time spent in REM.

Hollingworth's study was the first of many to come. Today we understand a great deal about how caffeine stimulates brain activity. It's a psychoactive stimulant that increases the actions of epinephrine and dopamine, in part by increasing the availability of dopamine receptors, the sites on cells where it can attach and thereby initiate its effects. Caffeine also increases the activity of certain neural circuits and brain areas associated with alertness, such as the locus coeruleus, which we discussed earlier in this chapter.

We also understand now how it interferes with sleep. That brings us back to adenosine. Caffeine is what is called an adenosine antagonist. It parks in adenosine receptors, which prevents adenosine from exerting its normal fatigue-inducing activity in the brain. As sleep expert Matthew Walker describes it, "Caffeine keeps pulling out the chairs from under adenosine." So even though adenosine is building up with each hour we are awake and increasingly so when we are very alert or active, our brains don't register that fatigue or the number of hours we've been awake accurately. Caffeine dampens the communication between adenosine and the brain. This process explains the phenomenon many of us know of as the caffeine crash. Once caffeine's actions on those receptors wear off, which our metabolism accomplishes in a few hours, the non-receptor-bound adenosine that has accumulated suddenly can bind and fatigue hits us. In addition, caffeine makes our brain more active and increases our capacity for physical effort, and that generates more adenosine as a byproduct, which in turn means the crash is harder than it would be without caffeine.

This all sounds rough, but I want to reiterate: I love caffeine and I have no plans to give it up. The data say caffeine in moderation is fine... and may even be good for us. Many of the benefits from coffee and tea are not from caffeine but from antioxidants contained in coffee beans and certain teas. • If you drink, avoid alcohol within eight hours of the time you plan to be asleep. This timing reduces the amount of alcohol in your body by the time you go to bed.

Alcohol has also been found to decrease the amount of growth hormone and testosterone released during the night—hormones critical for vitality and metabolism for both men and women. Normally, growth hormone is released relatively soon after falling asleep, and testosterone is released before and during REM sleep. The negative effects of alcohol on REM and these hormones happen acutely, meaning after even just a single night of drinking or for those who are alcohol sensitive, even one drink. Chronic drinking is even more problematic for sleep. Insomnia and alcohol dependency frequently coexist, for example. Beyond the changes one or two drinks can make on REM sleep, people with alcohol dependency tend to have decreased amounts of both N2 and N3 sleep, the non-REM period when we sink into a deep sleep. Frequent drinking also interferes with our circadian rhythm, disrupting or even decreasing the amount of melatonin our brains produce.

Adolescents are at particular risk of turning to alcohol intake as a sleep aid. In 2008, public health researchers at the University of Texas Health Science Center reported their findings from a large, yearlong study of insomnia among youth between the ages of eleven and seventeen years. They collected data on 3,134 people in this age range from a baseline date and then twelve months later and found that chronic insomnia heightened the risk of alcohol use. That's concerning because insomnia is the most common sleep disorder among young people, and because nighttime phone use, which is very common in this age group, also interferes with sleep quality and duration. Phone use at night has been linked to insomnia. That means there are two major risks to this age group when it comes to good sleep, not to mention the chronic stress that kids at that age face. Occasional alcohol use closer to bedtime, say once a month or less, is very unlikely to cause long-term problems, unless it's excessive during that once-a-month night out. If you drink in the eight hours before sleep, make sure you also consume sufficient water before going to sleep and after waking. Take electrolytes too if you can, and emphasize other behaviors that support great sleep, as well as a healthy microbiome, to try to offset the effects of alcohol.

To be clear, it's good to enjoy life. If having a few drinks during a celebration or a night out now and again is how you do, you're not alone. The important considerations are that this isn't happening too often, that you're not driving, that you're not experiencing any kind of dependency, and that you're not too young to drink (the negative effects of alcohol are much worse for the developing brain compared to the adult brain).

Not with respect to the negative effects on sleep and the microbiome. As mentioned above, no alcohol is better than any alcohol. Although many studies have been done on the potential benefits of red wine, conclusive evidence of this link does not exist. The amount of red wine you would need to drink to get benefits from grape skin, for example, would require consumption of enough alcohol to far outweigh any benefits. Put simply, the interaction between alcohol and our sleep processes is the same regardless of the drink.

Also, people who sleep with their phones in their rooms with the ringer on contributed to the numbers reported in the study, indicating that the problem isn't just about late-night scrolling.

We have known since at least the 1970s that the bedroom should be reserved for sleep and intimacy. The evidence linking various stimuli to insomnia is well established. Yet decades later, here we are, with about 1,350 out of 1,508 randomly selected Americans ignoring this basic practice.

A Tip Sheet for Avoiding Jet Lag

Some people experience terrible jet lag, others far less so. This changes as we age. And it depends on where we fly—which direction and if we need to push ourselves to wake earlier or stay awake later than usual. The latter is always easier for people.
Five factors allow you to shift your circadian clock. Knowing these can help you switch to a new time zone quickly, which allows you to be more effective on work trips and enjoy vacations more fully.
The factors you use to entrain your SCN to a new local light-dark cycle are, in descending order of influence:
• Light
• Temperature
• Meal times
• Exercise
• Social factors

You might think: Can't I just hop on the local schedule? Alas, that's hard because your SCN is entrained to wherever you have been for the prior week or so before your trip. So for instance if you fly from California to London and arrive at 5:00

by using light, exercise, and caffeine. In this case, however, you'll want to shift everything thirty to forty-five minutes later in the day as opposed to earlier. A slightly later wake-up time, a slightly later caffeine intake in the morning and early afternoon (but still avoid caffeine in the eight to ten hours prior to bedtime), and a slightly later workout—even just by forty-five minutes—will all help. You'll also want to make sure that you view bright light from artificial lights one to two hours after sunset. Remember, you're trying to prepare to stay up later as you soon fly westward.
WHEN YOU ARRIVE AT YOUR NEW DESTINATION (REGARDLESS OF WHETHER YOU FLEW EAST OR WEST)

• Eat like a local. Adopting the local meal schedule when you arrive—eating breakfast, lunch, and dinner more or less at the same times as the locals, even if you're not hungry—will help you shift your circadian clock to the new time zone. Personally, I hate to eat when I'm not hungry (and love to eat when I am!), so I opt out of this protocol. If it works for you, go for it. The sooner you can get on the local meal schedule, the better. Many find it effective to fast for a period of fourteen to sixteen hours before the local breakfast time so they are very hungry when that time arrives.

• Time your light exposure correctly by knowing your temperature minimum. This is the real power tool to shift your circadian clock fast, but it involves learning your temperature minimum first. See Sleep Protocol 3 and Sleep Protocol 5 for more on that topic.

For now, know that it occurs approximately two hours before your usual wake-up time. If you typically wake up at 7:00 a.m., your temperature minimum is very likely to be between 4:30 a.m. and 5:30 a.m. Here's the key: If you get bright light exposure in the one to two hours after your temperature minimum, you will adjust your circadian clock such that it will make you want to go to sleep earlier on the subsequent nights and wake up earlier on the subsequent mornings. Perfect for traveling east. Conversely, if you get bright light exposure in the one to two hours before your temperature minimum, you will shift your circadian clock such that it will make you want to go to sleep later on the subsequent nights and wake up later on the subsequent mornings. Perfect for traveling west. But remember we are referring to the time of your temperature minimum before you leave! This is vital to understand. Get it right and you'll shift fast across time zones. Get it wrong and it can be a mess. Why? Well, think about this. Imagine you fly from San Francisco to London (+8 hours). You land in the morning London time and the sun is out. I said get morning sunlight in your eyes, right? Yes, but for the first two to three days in London before you adjust your clock, viewing that London morning sunlight is the same to your brain's clock as getting a giant blast of light in your eyes at midnight San Francisco time. So you just made your body want to go to bed much later and wake up later. You got it backward.

Many people sleep well their first night after flying east, wake up, see sunlight, and the second night is a mess. They can't sleep! It would be better to wear dark sunglasses during the two to three hours before your temperature minimum for the first two days in London. After those first two or three days, just view sunlight per the recommendations earlier in this chapter. Obviously, I am just using London as an example. • Use artificial light and blue and green (short wavelength) blocking glasses as tools. Of course, it's often very cloudy, or you may land at night, and we can't control the time of sunrise and sunset—though if you can, please contact me. What you can do, however, is travel with a portable bright light device (you'll want one with 5,000- to 10,000-lux brightness) to shift your circadian clock. Several are the size of a book and thin enough to fit in a carry-on bag. I have no affiliation with any companies that make these, but I use the Verilux Happy Light when I travel. They cost about $50. At home I use a larger countertop unit, the Carex Daylight (also no affiliation) and Ra Optics or Bon Charge full-spectrum LED bulbs in the daytime, as discussed earlier.

Remember that even when it is cloudy, sunlight through cloud cover is still almost always far brighter than artificial lighting. Get outside and view that sunlight at the correct times and you'll shift your circadian clock fast. Then, you can return to the standard protocols to stay on the local schedule.

One more thing we can all control is the brightness of our evening and nighttime environment. As you get ready for bed, reduce exposure to bright lights—especially blue and green, or short-wavelength, light. Alas, as you now know, all LED lights are rich in blue and green wavelengths. For that reason, I wear blue and green (short wavelength) blocking glasses after sundown to help adjust to the local schedule. This protocol is known to protect against the melatonin-reducing effects of bright light and to prevent the cortisol-increasing effects of bright light.
• Maintain a regular exercise schedule. While traveling, try to maintain a consistent early-in-the-day exercise routine (adjusted to the local schedule). That, too, helps shift your circadian clock.
• A final tip. For trips that last fewer than two days, staying on (or near) your home sleep-wake, eating, and exercise schedule can be beneficial to minimize disruptions to your circadian rhythm.

These tips will help you quickly overcome any jet lag in your future travels—they've certainly helped me over the years, as well as people in the military, medical professions working night shifts, and more.
